title: On the trail of the artist

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The special character of the ridges or lines on our fingers has been recognised for thousands of years. The study of prehistoric pottery, for example, reveals the utilisation of fingerprint impressions in the clay as a potter's mark, and hand prints have been found on ancient cave painting. But it was only in the nineteenth century that a failsafe method was developed to identify and classify the features of individual prints, allowing them to be used in crime detection. Fingerprints then became an important source of evidence in courts of law. More recently, however, another application has been found for this branch of forensic science.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: With works by some artists changing hands for millions of dollars, it can be vital to know whether or not a painting was actually produced by the artist to whom it is attributed. This is where evidence from fingerprints can be enormously valuable. Paintings and other works of art frequently preserve the marks of the hands and fingers that created them. The artist may have used his or her fingertip to lift off unwanted deposits of paint, or to smooth out marks left by the brush while the paint was still wet. In some instances, the finger was actually used to apply the colour, stamping a fine network of ridges onto the painting. And artists often varnished their own paintings, creating another opportunity to leave identifiable marks behind.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In crime detection, fingerprints found at the scene of the crime are compared with those of a suspected criminal. If they match, this is strong evidence that the suspect was involved in the crime. In the case of a work of art, however, the 'suspect' is often no longer available – he or she may have lived hundreds of years ago. So for the identification of an artist to take place, the fingerprints on the painting under question must be compared with other prints which are definitely those of the artist. Another work which is known to be by the artist concerned has therefore to be examined. If usable prints exist here and a match is found, the attribution can be tentatively confirmed.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The authentication of a painting by the English artist J M W Turner painted in the late 1820s and entitled Landscape with Rainbow is a good illustration of this process. The painting was only re-discovered in the 1980s, but at first it was not thought to be by Turner. When it was being cleaned, a print was discovered where the artist had used his fingertip to smooth wet paint. A cross-match was identified between this fingerprint and one found on another painting, Chichester Canal. This hangs in the Tate Britain Gallery in London, and has an unquestionable provenance all the way back to the artist. The accuracy of the match was confirmed by police specialists, and the newly discovered painting, originally bought for a few hundred dollars, finally sold for close to $200,000.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In another case, a sketch of a woman's head was found on a folded piece of paper inside an old envelope bought with some other papers from an antique shop. It was executed in red chalk with an inscription written in brown ink. The design was faded and worn and the paper was yellowed and contaminated. The newly discovered drawing strongly resembled another sketch, the Head of St Anne by the sixteenth-century Italian artist Leonardo da Vinci, which has been in the British Royal Collection since 1629. This was one of a series of studies made by Leonardo for a later oil painting. Investigators found the scale of the two drawings was different, so offsetting (copying by direct transference) could not have been used to produce the new drawing. Differences also existed in the design itself, principally in the folds of the clothing and in the angle of the head. But overall the drawings were similar enough to make experts wonder if the newly discovered sketch could be by the same hand.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: When the paper was examined, several fingerprints were noticed on the back. However, no analysis was done at the time due to a lack of fingerprint data for Leonardo's works. But by chance, a few months after the discovery of the drawing, an unusually good-quality photograph of Leonardo's oil painting St Jerome, which is in the Vatican Museum in Rome, revealed several prints left in the paint where the fingertip had been used to smooth the paint while it was still wet. Since scholars generally agree that Leonardo painted St Jerome, the conclusion that these prints are his would be hard to argue against. The fingerprints were compared with those on the newly discovered drawing, and it was found that both were created by the same finger. This is powerful circumstantial evidence that dates the drawing of the woman's head to Leonardo's lifetime and proves that Leonardo physically handled the paper. Combined with the artistic quality of the drawing, Leonardo's involvement beyond the mere handling of the paper is indicated.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: It must be stressed that a match in the above cases does not 'prove' authorship in the rigorous sense of the word proof. It does, however, offer valuable circumstantial evidence that can complement a scholar's or expert's assessment of a work of art.
